### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of modern contract law doctrine is firmly rooted in the philosophical foundations of the Enlightenment—an era in which human beings were idealized as autonomous rational agents, a *homo economicus* standing atop the tower of their own cognition, capable of clear cost-benefit calculations without systematic external distortion. In the classical architecture of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*), particularly Article 1320, the validity of an agreement hinges upon four fundamental conditions: the consent of the parties bound thereby, their capacity to enter into an engagement, a specific subject matter, and a lawful cause. Among these four pillars, the first and second conditions—namely consent (*toestemming*) and capacity—form the most sacred bulwark of legal subjects' sovereignty. Consent is presumed to arise from a free will (*vrije wil*), an emanation of internal autonomy uncontaminated by pressure, error, fraud, or undue influence. Classical legal epistemology views the will as a transparent entity that can be objectively tested through its external manifestations. When an individual signs a contract or clicks an acceptance button, the law presumptively assumes a complete synchronization between internal volition and physical declaration in the external world—a doctrine frequently elaborated in the German tradition through the *Willenstheorie*, juxtaposed alongside the *Verklaringstheorie*.

However, this transparent epistemology collapses spectacularly as we enter the socio-technological landscape of the 21st century—an era where human interaction is totally mediated by artificial intelligence-based autonomous agents and highly sophisticated computational architectures of persuasion. Today, legal subjects no longer transact across a neutral wooden desk with negotiating partners of equivalent cognitive capacity. Instead, we inhabit a digital ecosystem populated by dark patterns, predictive algorithms, and large language models capable of identifying a subject's psychological vulnerabilities in real time. In this context, autonomous agents are no longer mere passive tools like the quill pens or mechanical calculators of the past; they are active participants possessing artificial agency, specifically engineered to influence the probability of human decision-making through the manipulation of emotional and cognitive latent spaces. When an artificial intelligence system designs an interface that neurologically triggers dopamine releases, obscures pricing information, or exploits the user's cognitive bias toward loss aversion, where lies the freedom of will championed by classical jurists? This question demands a radical deconstruction of the foundational assumptions of private law.

Genealogically, we are witnessing a paradigm shift from the contract grounded in pure autonomy (*autonomous contract*) toward what may be termed the algorithmically-induced contract. Our civil law is trapped in a snare of philosophical anachronism: it utilizes nineteenth-century lenses to evaluate transactions occurring within the digital matrix of the twenty-first century. When Article 1320 formulated consent, its drafters—such as J.E. de Jonge and the framers of the colonial Indonesian Civil Code—could never have imagined a scenario where human decision-making processes are mapped through neural networks trained on billions of behavioral data points, yielding a rate of manipulative success far exceeding the persuasive capacities of conventional humans. Furthermore, if we dissect theoretical works such as those written by P. Scholten regarding legal discovery (*rechtsfinding*), civil law must not be allowed to become a doctrinal fossil blind to social reality. Therefore, a doctrinal dissection of Article 1320 in the era of autonomous agents is not merely a cosmetic academic exercise, but an urgent epistemological necessity to rescue the integrity of contractual justice from the threat of the digital colonization of the human psyche.
